beats.spoken: Wednesday, 10:05 a.m. A supplier sends a quote. Your AI assistant is set to summarise it. The document contains a sentence you can't see.

To you, it all looks normal: a quote, a PDF, a tidy summary. The UK's NCSC calls prompt injection one of the most reported weaknesses of today's language models. And according to OWASP, the instruction can be invisible to people.

fact.text: Instructions in a document can be invisible to people.

beats.spoken: Your assistant can also send emails. What do you do? A: Everything keeps running automatically. B: You only trust known senders. C: Sending and paying only after your approval. Remember your choice.

options.text: Send and pay only with approval

beats.spoken: Let's play out A. The assistant reads the quote, and the hidden sentence with it. If it's vulnerable, it follows it. An email goes out that you never wrote. You only notice when a customer asks about it.

The right answer is C. OWASP advises giving the AI only the permissions it really needs, and having a human approve high-risk actions. A grants too much. B doesn't reliably help, because instructions can hide in any outside content.
For today: check which accounts your AI tool can reach. Set sending and paying to approval. And read results before they go out.
